clue.text: Titled rank-and the rest might be lost for promotion

definitions.text: Titled rank-and the rest might be lost for promotion

parts.words: Titled rank-and the rest might be lost for promotion
parts.note: a hereditary title held by a 'Sir' who is not a peer; promoted to a peerage, its holder becomes a baron, and the tail of the title's word (the 'etc.' and the rest) falls away

explanation.surface: A nobleman's title that he might give up on being raised higher.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the ETCY from the end of the word and BARON is left: being promoted to baron loses 'the rest', which is ETC (etcetera) plus a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A baronet's hereditary status, below the peerage, is a titled rank in the British honours system.

clue.text: Barrels used in shooting

definitions.meaning: large casks for wine or beer
mounds behind targets on an archery or rifle range

explanation.surface: Casks used at a shooting range.
explanation.definitionFit: Large casks for ale and the targets' earth mounds at a range share this word.

clue.text: Right, poorly, and getting abusive

parts.note: poorly means ill, unwell

explanation.surface: Someone sick and growing foul-mouthed.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail at someone is to scold them bitterly, so a railing tirade is abusive.

clue.text: Uses a neat concoction that is disgusting

indicators.note: a concoction is a mixture, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A drinker taking spirits neat in a revolting mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To be disgusting to someone is to make them feel sick, the verb used here.

clue.text: Natural idolatry of family pride'

definitions.meaning: pagan devotion to sacred trees
read as reverence for one's family tree

explanation.surface: Asking about a natural form of idolatry rooted in family pride.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverence for sacred woods is a pagan cult, and veneration of a genealogy is a lineage-proud vanity.

clue.text: Wage rise'? Just talk

indicators.note: in a down clue a rise reads the word upwards, so backwards

parts.note: pay is a wage

explanation.surface: Asking for a pay increase is mere chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' looks like a wage increase, but in this down clue it turns PAY upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle chatter or noisy jabber, mere gab without substance.

clue.text: Prelude in E, in concert

indicators.note: the second 'in' tells us the letter E sits inside the word for a concert

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at the London Proms

explanation.surface: A musical introduction written in the key of E, played at a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is part of the musical picture ('in E', a key); only the second places E inside PROM.
explanation.definitionFit: A proem is a preface or introductory passage, a formal word for an opening to a longer work.

clue.text: Falstaff: " I'll and leave sack, and live cleanly

definitions.text: Falstaff: " I'll and leave sack, and live cleanly

parts.words: Falstaff: " I'll and leave sack, and live cleanly
parts.note: Falstaff's promise of reform at the end of Henry IV Part 1: the missing word means cleanse himself

explanation.surface: Falstaff vowing to give up sherry and live a clean life.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is sherry, Falstaff's favourite drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleanse oneself of excesses, a word for clearing out impurities.

clue.text: Pantaloon, proverbially surpassing' younger rivals

definitions.meaning: the foolish old man of the commedia dell'arte and pantomime
the proverb says there is no fool like an aged one

explanation.surface: A pantomime character said to beat the younger competition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantaloon is the doddering old dupe of Italian comedy, and the proverb ranks him above any younger idiot.

clue.text: Ladies who limber up, by habit, in droves

indicators.note: in places the word for habit inside the word for crowds

parts.note: masses are droves or crowds
use is habit or custom

explanation.surface: Nuns in their habits flocking to exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habit' suggests a nun's dress, but it means custom; the 'Ladies' loosen others' muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: Women who give massages loosen and supple others' muscles.

clue.text: Newspaper leader ?

definitions.meaning: several papers carry this title, such as the Chicago one
in ancient Rome an officer elected to protect and lead the plebeians

explanation.surface: A question about the editorial column of a paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a newspaper title and a Roman people's champion, a leader of the commons.

clue.text: Sets out ostentatiously for walks

definitions.meaning: displays something showily, flaunts it
promenades or public walkways, or processions on foot

explanation.surface: Someone showing off while out for a stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: To flaunt is to display showily, and seafront promenades are also called by this word.

clue.text: Music rooms ?

definitions.meaning: an instrumental work in several movements, such as a dance sequence
a set of connected rooms in a hotel

explanation.surface: A query about rooms set aside for music.
explanation.definitionFit: A multi-movement instrumental piece and a hotel's set of connected chambers share this name.

clue.text: Trouble hence is looking glum

parts.note: woe is trouble or misfortune
'hence!' is an old command meaning go away, be off

explanation.surface: Someone troubled and therefore wearing a long face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hence' looks like 'therefore', but here it is the archaic order to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorrowful and dejected in appearance, wearing a miserable expression.

clue.text: Backing which motorists try to steer clear of

definitions.meaning: support or approval

definitions.text: which motorists try to steer clear of
definitions.meaning: a penalty mark recorded on a driving licence

explanation.surface: Support of a kind that drivers try to avoid.
explanation.definitionFit: Approval or support, and a penalty recorded on a British driving licence, share the word.

clue.text: A funny thing, silence

definitions.meaning: a joke or comic line
to stop someone speaking, as with a cloth over the mouth

explanation.surface: A comedian's line, followed by silence.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedian's joke and a muzzle for the mouth both go by this short word.

clue.text: Cycle attachments for one's luggage?

definitions.meaning: covers fitted over a bicycle's chain and gearing
read as boxes for one's gear, belongings

explanation.surface: Bicycle fittings for carrying baggage.
explanation.definitionFit: Housings enclosing a bicycle's chain mechanism, and read literally, boxes for kit.

clue.text: Harper's place takes in manufactured yarns

parts.note: the song 'The harp that once through Tara's halls' puts the harper at Tara, the seat of Ireland's ancient kings
to take someone in is to cheat or swindle them, to diddle them

explanation.surface: A harpist's home that is full of invented stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes in' looks like a container signal, but it is a charade piece meaning cheats.
explanation.definitionFit: Made-up tales are fibs or petty lies, which is what this old word means.

clue.text: Debts surrounding a game for pearly queens

indicators.note: surrounding means the word for debts goes round the game

parts.note: dues are debts, sums owed
chess is a board game

explanation.surface: Money owed around a game played by Cockney royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearly kings and queens are London costermongers in button-covered clothes; 'duchess' is Cockney slang for a wife.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney slang a 'duchess' is a wife, the costermonger's queen.

clue.text: Such pressure from the Homeric past, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters given could form something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking whether a certain pressure comes from Homer's ancient world.
explanation.definitionFit: Air pressure is the pressure exerted by the air around the Earth, named after the surrounding air.

clue.text: Not wanted by Tennyson when sailing

definitions.text: Not wanted by Tennyson when sailing

parts.words: Not wanted by Tennyson when sailing
parts.note: from 'Crossing the Bar': 'And may there be no ... of the bar, When I put out to sea'

explanation.surface: Something a poet did not wish for on his voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamenting or groaning, the sound the poet hoped the sandbar would not make.

clue.text: Urgent appeal is nothing short of moderate

indicators.note: short of means lacking something, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: so-so means middling or moderate
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: An emergency request is anything but mild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nothing short of' reads as 'absolutely', but it says SO-SO lacks one O.
explanation.definitionFit: The Morse distress signal is the standard plea for help at sea.

clue.text: Exquisite female, seeing badly, takes nothing in

indicators.note: takes, with 'in', means one piece holds another inside it
badly says the letters are put wrongly, so rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A fine woman with poor eyesight letting nothing in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges SEEING into SIGNEE, which 'takes' O in.
explanation.definitionFit: The French feminine form means well-groomed and elegant, said of a woman.

clue.text: Sourpuss, to decry Atalanta's pick-up

parts.note: to crab is to criticise or run down
in Greek myth Atalanta lost her race by stopping to pick up golden apples

explanation.surface: A grumpy person criticising the heroine of a Greek myth.
explanation.walkthrough: Atalanta was the runner whom Hippomenes beat by dropping golden apples she stopped to gather.
explanation.definitionFit: The small wild fruit is very sour, and the word also names a crabby, bad-tempered person.

clue.text: A legend (in two parts) appears stirring

parts.note: split in two, leg-end: the end of a leg

explanation.surface: A myth told in two parts is in progress.
explanation.walkthrough: '(in two parts)' says to split 'legend' into 'leg end'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something underway or astir is in motion, in progress.

clue.text: Invite perhaps a hundred — then chuck them out

annotationWithheld.why: Invite perhaps a hundred - then chuck them out: INVITE plus C (a hundred) rearranged gives EVICT plus IN; no clue word supplies the IN to be removed unless 'chuck them out' is both definition and deletion signal
annotationWithheld.clue: Invite perhaps a hundred — then chuck them out

clue.text: 3'Slightly saccharine little daughter in the river

parts.note: twee means sweet in a cloying way
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A sugary little girl paddling in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The river runs along the border between England and Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A Border waterway, the stream that also names a woollen cloth.

clue.text: Proverbial polygamists, every man Jack of them

definitions.meaning: seamen are said to have a wife in every port
a Jack, or Jack tar, is a seaman

explanation.surface: Every one of a group of men famed for many marriages.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamen are proverbially wed in every harbour, and each one is a 'Jack tar'.

clue.text: Droop in folds again

indicators.note: in shows the letters lie within these clue words

explanation.surface: Sagging in the creases once more.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink or hang down limply, to go slack.

clue.text: Scent of peculiar quality

definitions.meaning: a perfume or concentrated extract
the intrinsic nature that makes a thing what it is, 'peculiar' meaning particular to it

explanation.surface: A perfume with an odd character.
explanation.definitionFit: A concentrated perfume extract and the core nature of something share this name.

clue.text: With which and what one sees

definitions.text: With which and what one sees

parts.words: With which and what one sees
parts.note: names both the faculty of the eyes and a spectacle or view

explanation.surface: A riddle about the means and the object of seeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Vision is the faculty of seeing, and a spectacle or view is also called by this word.

clue.text: Football crowds to lead in Durham

parts.note: a gate is the number of spectators at a match
to head is to lead, be at the front

explanation.surface: Football fans heading for the lead in a northern county.
explanation.walkthrough: The town on the Tyne opposite Newcastle was historically in County Durham, in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: This Tyneside town stood within the historic county of Durham, so it is a place found there.
